extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and clergy interested in the authenticity and credibility of Christian scriptures (e.g., theologians, critics, literate lay Christians)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the authenticity, canonical status, and credibility of biblical books and miracle reports, emphasizing witness quality, early attestation, provenance, internal consistency, and motives for forgery. The text offers historical-critical principles for accepting or rejecting scriptural claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old Testament as sole true canon
rubrics_metrics.description: The Old Testament is at this moment the sole true canon of Scripture, acknowledged as such by genuine Christianity; it was the only canon which was acknowledged by Christ, and his immediate Apostles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the criterion that canonical status must trace to the recognition of Jesus and the apostles; if a book was not treated as 'Scripture' by them, its claim to canonical authority is weakened. The New Testament should be evaluated in light of whether it was regarded as equivalent to the Old Testament by earliest authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon must be declared by Jesus or his apostles
rubrics_metrics.description: If Christianity required a new canon, or new digest of laws, it ought to have been done by Jesus and his apostles, and not left to be executed by any after them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to direct apostolic declaration when judging the legitimacy of a canon. Later declarations by fathers or councils are suspect if no apostolic endorsement exists; the legitimacy of a canon is reduced when established long after the founders' deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early and contemporaneous attestation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the first hundred years after the lives of the supposed authors, none at all [testimony of the gospels' authors].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require early, near-contemporary testimony for strong claims about authorship and authenticity. Absence of attestation in the immediate generations after the purported authors is a significant reason for skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the New Testament writings (occasional/commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The books of the New Testament are all occasional books, and not a code or system of religion; nor were they all collected into one body, nor declared by any even human authority to be all canonical till several hundred years after Jesus Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess genre and purpose: if writings are occasional commentaries rather than legislative or foundational codices, they have different claims to universal canonical authority. Treat 'occasional' works with caution when inferring doctrinal or canonical status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal signs of forgery and contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The gospels are accused of being written by credulous and superstitious authors whose names are not certainly known; as containing too inconsistent and contradictory accounts of prodigies and miracles; and also palpable marks of forgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine texts for internal inconsistencies, contradictory accounts, and textual markers of forgery; such defects are grounds for rejecting claims of authentic apostolic authorship or divine origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and character of witnesses (patristic credibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient Fathers were extremely credulous and superstitious, possessed with strong prejudices... they were roundly affirming as true things evidently false and fictitious; ... they would not scruple to propagate any fiction... and have been palpably liars, cheats, and forgers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the trustworthiness of patristic witnesses: if the fathers are shown to have propagated forgeries or to have been credulous, their testimony for the authenticity of texts and miracles is seriously undermined. Investigate known instances where fathers accepted or produced spurious works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of evidence: witness quality must scale with importance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an obvious rule in the admission of evidence in any cause whatsoever, that the more important the matter to be determined by it is, the more unsullied, and unexceptionable ought to be the characters of the witnesses to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply proportional standards of evidence: extraordinary or world-historical claims (e.g., miracles, canonical status) require testimony from unimpeachable witnesses. Do not accept testimony in matters of the highest importance from witnesses who would be excluded in ordinary tribunals for lack of credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of widespread imposture and credulity weakens miracle reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The age in which the accounts of these miracles were published, was an age overflowing with imposture and credulity... Such was the license of fiction in the first ages, and so easy the credulity, that testimony of the facts of that time is to be received with great caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When miracle reports originate in an historical milieu known for fabrications, popular credulity, and fictional storytelling, treat those reports skeptically. Consider cultural propensity for miracle-making as a disconfirming context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of many spurious books and sectarian disputes undermines canonical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The church in its first ages was full of forged books... The different sects, and the church itself, was torn by as many schisms then as it ever has been since, who mutually accuse each other of corrupting the Christians scriptures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the multiplicity of competing texts and sectarian claims: when many forgeries and variant narratives circulated, singular claims to an authoritative canon carry less force. Consider the process of selection and the factious environment as evidence against unambiguous authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives and interests (pious fraud) can produce false testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: When disposed to speak the truth, [the fathers] have not scrupled to confess, that the miraculous shifts were then actually withdrawn... yet they would not scruple to propagate any fiction... to promote the interest either of Christianity in general, or of any particular rite or doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate possible motives (defense of faith, promotion of rites, consolidation of authority) that could have prompted fabrication or embellishment. Testimony arising from partisan or self-interested motives is less reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not insist on extraordinary acceptance where ordinary evidence is lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: And when we consider the character of those by whom these histories were first received and believed, the unreasonableness of insisting upon the belief of these accounts will appear aggravated... I cannot... without renouncing all those rules and principles of evidence, and of good sense, which in all other cases are universally respected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ordinary standards of evidence and common-sense rules when evaluating religious-historical claims; do not demand assent when the evidentiary standards used in other domains would rightly prevent belief.
